newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Mandela says economic growth crucial to democracy.
newsitem.headline: Mandela says economic growth crucial to democracy.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela on Sunday urged closer economic ties with Asia, saying democracy in his country would remain fragile if it did not lift the country's economy and unite its once feuding communities.

"Our democracy will remain fragile, and our rights mere formalities if they do not bring improvement in the lives of people, and if we do not reconcile those once torn apart," Mandela told academics at the University of the Philippines.
"That is why our visit to southeast Asia is focused with such intent on issues of trade and investment," Mandela said in an acceptance speech after the University conferred on him an honorary degree.
Mandela's Asian trip, on which he is accompanied by a business delegation and by his Mozambican female companion, will also cover Brunei, Malaysia and Singapore.
"Sustainable and higher rates of growth are central to fulfilling South Africa's plans for reconstruction and development," Mandela said.

Later in an address to members of the Makati Business Club, the country's premier group of businessmen, Mandela said he hoped his visit would lead to greater economic cooperation within the two regions.

"In a world increasingly organised into regional economic blocs, stronger links between Philippines and South Africa would bring the added value of strengthening bonds between Southern Africa and southeast Asia, between SADC and ASEAN," Mandela said.

The SADC (Southern African Development Community) which groups Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe, represents 40 percent of the population of the African continent and more than 80 percent of Africa's GNP.

The ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) which has among its members the world's fastest growing economies, groups Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Brunei, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
"They (ASEAN and SADC) belong to nations which ... together have the power to give strong impetus to the rebirth of relations between Africa and Asia," Mandela said.
Mandela was accompanied for the first time on a state visit by his companion Graca Machel, the 51-year-old widow of former Mozambican president Samora Machel.
Officials of the South African delegation said trade relations with the Philippines were still very minimal and the two sides were exploring opportunities.
"I think the visit to Malaysia will be very important because we are looking for large investments," an official who did not want to be named said.
Officials of South Africa's North West Province said they were seeking investments in tourism, mining, manufacturing, agriculture, food industries, venture capital and pharmaceuticals.
Mandela leaves for Brunei on Monday where he will spend two days before going to Singapore and Malaysia.
